title: Algorithmic Foundations for Multi-Objective Learning and Decision-Making | EECS at UC Berkeley
content: Algorithmic Foundations for Multi-Objective Learning and Decision-Making | EECS at UC Berkeley Algorithmic Foundations for Multi-Objective Learning and Decision-Making Eric Zhao EECS Department, University of California, Berkeley Technical Report No. UCB/EECS-2025-173 September 9, 2025 http://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2025/EECS-2025-173.pdf Machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in real-world decision-making roles where they must simultaneously fulfill multiple objectives. This departure from machine learning's roots in single-objective pattern recognition calls for revisiting the conceptual frameworks that we use to reason about, design, and deploy these systems. In this dissertation, we present three thrusts toward building a foundational understanding of multi-objective machine learning and decision-making. The first part of this work presents deep dives into fundamental challenges in balancing multiple objectives during decision-making. We begin by studying how to balance between objectives that must be learned from different data sources, and introduce a framework of multi-distribution learning to formalize this problem. We then consider how to balance among conflicting objectives that operate on different time scales, using content recommendation algorithms as a case study. The second part explores the multi-objective foundations of forecasting: predicting the likelihood of future events to inform downstream decisions. We first introduce a general algorithmic framework unifying a class of forecasting algorithms that guarantee calibration for multiple observers simultaneously. We then revisit the fundamental question of how to evaluate a forecaster's performance and construct a best-of-all-worlds evaluation scheme that averages over randomly sampled calibration objectives. The third part focuses on language models and how their multi-task training shapes their capabilities. We first investigate the heterogeneous effectiveness of finetuning and highlight the importance of multi-task diversity in finetuning data. We then explore how verification capabilities interact with problem-solving capabilities in reasoning models, and probe the ceiling that self-verification imposes on the scalability of sampling-based search.
